newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian mediator meets rebels in steady talks.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian mediator meets rebels in steady talks.

text.p: A key mediator met Peruvian rebels holding 72 hostages on Saturday in the latest round of peace talks zeroing in on rebel demands for freedom for their jailed comrades, sources close to the talks said.

Carrying a folder bulging with papers, Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani walked into the besieged Japanese ambassador's house in Lima and left about an hour later, without the folder and without comment.

Cipriani has carried out a daily shuttle diplomacy this week between President Alberto Fujimori's office and the mined and booby-trapped residence in the rich suburb of San Isidro, looking for a solution to the 116-day standoff.

The visit followed a three-hour meeting Thursday between Cipriani, two other mediators and the leader of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) hostage-takers, Nestor Cerpa, at a safe house across the street from the residence.
"We are moving ahead on the right track," Cipriani told reporters after the Thursday evening meeting, confirming also that Cerpa led the guerrilla side in the talks.

It was thought to be the first time an MRTA representative had left the house for talks since March 12, when both sides refused to budge on the MRTA's demands for freedom for hundreds of jailed comrades.
Fujimori, whom officials say is personally leading the government negotiation drive with little help from advisers, flew to the Amazon jungle town of Nauta to open a new highway.
Sources close to talks said the two sides were engaged in delicate behind-the-scenes haggling over the rebels' main demand for the freedom for MRTA fighters in Peruvian jails.
"There is talk of liberation for some of the small fry and reduction of sentences ... some of them may have exaggerated sentences," said a political source close to the government Friday.

Fujimori has steadfastly refused to release any convicted MRTA fighters -- and sources saw no chance of him softening that stand. But talks were focusing on possible sentence reductions for low-ranking MRTA prisoners, or release of those detained but not convicted, they said.

"There is a will to reach an agreement," said the same source. He added there may be some ransom payment to the MRTA as part of an overall deal but that "the government does not want to talk about that."

"The payment of a ransom is one condition that neither side will talk about. It's in neither side's interest to discuss it publicly," said the former chief of Peru's terrorism police, Hector Jhon Caro, recently.

About 20 MRTA fighters swept into the Japanese ambassador's home during a cocktail party Dec. 17 and took all 500 guests hostage. They gradually released all but 72 of them, keeping a key list including Peru's foreign minister, Fujimori's brother and top Japanese businessmen.
Despite the plodding pace of talks, the political source said both sides remained committed to reaching agreement and that the MRTA realised its options were limited.
"If they are captured, they will go to jail on life sentences and will never see the sun again. They have to negotiate," he said.
Fujimori has already arranged political asylum for the rebels in Cuba and the Dominican Republic in the event of a peaceful outcome.
